title: Fruits With the Most Water

seo.title: Fruits With the Most Water by Percentage
seo.meta_description: Watermelon and strawberries are about 91% water, cantaloupe around 90%, peaches about 89%, and grapefruit near 88%. Fruit also contributes fiber and micronutrients.
seo.search_intent: Compare which fresh fruits contain the highest percentage of water.

excerpt: Watermelon and strawberries are among the most water-rich fruits at about 91% water. Cantaloupe is around 90%, peaches about 89%, grapefruit roughly 88%, and oranges around 87%. Two hundred grams of watermelon therefore contains about 182 grams of water.
content_html:
Fruit is not just sugar, fiber, and vitamins. In many fruits, roughly nine out of every ten grams are water. That helps explain their volume and relatively low energy density.

Especially water-rich fruits

Fresh fruitApprox. water
Watermelon~91%
Strawberries~91%
Cantaloupe~90%
Peach~89%
Grapefruit~88%
Orange~87%

Values are rounded and vary modestly with cultivar and ripeness.

What that means in a serving

If you eat 200 g of watermelon at 91% water, about 182 g of that serving is water. A couple of strawberries obviously contribute much less total fluid than a large bowl even if the percentages are similar.

Does fruit replace drinking water?

Fruit contributes meaningfully to hydration, but there is no need to treat it as a direct replacement for beverages. Water and other drinks remain the simplest way to meet fluid needs, while fruits, vegetables, soups, and other foods contribute too.

More water does not automatically mean “better hydration”

Watermelon, strawberries, melon and citrus can be well above 85–90% water, but the amount they actually provide depends on how much you eat. A 200 g serving of a fruit that is 90% water contains about 180 g of water; a small portion provides less even if its percentage is very high.

Fruit contributes to hydration alongside drinking water, other beverages and foods, while also providing natural sugars, fiber and micronutrients. The ranking describes composition; it is not a reason to routinely replace drinking water with fruit.

Dried fruit is the opposite case

Raisins and dates have lost much of their water, so sugars, calories, and minerals become far more concentrated per 100 g.

Watermelon is not “just water,” but its high water content explains much of its volume and low calorie density.

Hydration is more than a ranking of percentages

A fruit that is 90 percent water can contribute meaningfully to fluid intake, but eating it is not the same as drinking a glass of water. Fruit also contains carbohydrate, fiber, organic acids, minerals, and many plant compounds, and the solid structure slows the pace at which it is consumed. That combination is useful: watermelon, berries, melon, peaches, oranges, and similar fruits can make hydration more appealing while also providing nutrients that plain water does not contain.

The difference between 88 and 92 percent water is usually less important than serving size. Two hundred grams of watermelon supplies far more total water than a few slices of a slightly more water-dense fruit. This is why percentage tables are best used to understand relative composition, not to micromanage hydration. If you enjoy a particular fruit and eat a realistic portion of it, the amount on the plate matters more than winning a decimal-point contest.

Whole fruit also behaves differently from juice. Juicing retains much of the water and soluble material but removes or disrupts much of the intact fiber structure, making it easier to consume the sugars from several pieces of fruit quickly. A bowl of strawberries or melon requires chewing and has more volume for the same amount of carbohydrate than many juices. For routine hydration and snacking, whole fruit therefore offers practical advantages beyond its water percentage.

Season and storage can change texture and perceived juiciness even when database values look similar. A ripe peach can seem far juicier than an underripe one, and frozen berries release liquid as their cells thaw. Those changes do not mean the fruit has suddenly gained or lost most of its water; they change where the water is held and how readily it escapes. The database number is an average, not a promise about every individual piece.

Fruit should complement, not replace, regular fluids during heat, exercise, fever, or other situations with high water needs. A water-rich snack can help, especially for people who enjoy eating more than drinking, but thirst and fluid losses can exceed what a bowl of fruit can comfortably provide. The useful takeaway is simple: choose water-rich fruits because you like them and because they add fluid, fiber, and micronutrients—not because one fruit needs to be crowned the universal hydration champion.

Temperature affects appetite as well. Chilled melon, grapes, or citrus can be especially appealing in hot weather, which may indirectly help people eat more water-rich foods. That behavioral advantage is real even though it cannot be read from a composition table. The best hydrating fruit is often the one that is accessible, ripe, and enjoyable enough to eat in a meaningful portion.

faq.question: Which fruit has the most water?
faq.answer: Watermelon and strawberries are among the highest common fruits at roughly 91% water.

faq.question: Does cantaloupe have almost as much water as watermelon?
faq.answer: Yes. Cantaloupe is around 90%, very close to watermelon.

faq.question: Why is dried fruit so calorie-dense?
faq.answer: Drying removes water, concentrating sugars and calories into a smaller weight.
